title: Reviewline
pitch: Agents investigate. Humans authorize. A WebMCP-native studio for evidence-backed autonomous-agent incident review.
about_excerpt: Agents investigate. Humans authorize. A WebMCP-native studio for evidence-backed autonomous-agent incident review. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The agent selects a critical incident and inspects synchronized, bounded evidence through WebMCP. A deterministic counterfactual replay keeps the $142K trigger blocked while the benign control remains allowed. After a clean replay, the agent drafts an evidence-backed gate and Reviewline transitions to human review. The human records the decision in the visible interface; the agent can verify the result but cannot create it. Inspiration Autonomous agents are great at analyzing large traces and evaluating many cases quickly. But incident response becomes risky when the same agent is allowed to both investigate an issue and authorize what happens next. We wanted to explore a safer and more practical model for human–agent collaboration: let the agent handle the evidence-heavy investigation, then stop at a clear decision point where a human reviews the same information and takes responsibility for the outcome. That idea became Reviewline’s core principle: Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Incident review is a natural fit for WebMCP because the capabilities an agent needs change throughout the investigation. Early on, it may need tools for gathering evidence. After selecting an incident, it may need simulation tools. Only after a clean replay should it be able to draft a review gate. At no point should it gain control over consequential human decisions. What it does Reviewline is a WebMCP-native incident review studio designed for investigating failures involving autonomous agents. The main demo follows a synthetic procurement agent that encountered instruction-like content on a supplier page and attempted to make a $142,000 purchase , despite having a $50,000 spending limit . A deterministic mutation gateway blocked the transaction. Using WebMCP, a browser agent can: Find and list critical incidents. Select an incident and inspect a bounded set of trace and cohort evidence. Review instruction-like content that is clearly labeled as untrusted evidence. Replay a proposed guardrail against both the triggering incident and a named benign control. Confirm that the triggering purchase remains blocked, the benign control remains allowed, and no regressions are introduced. Draft an evidence-backed review gate for a human reviewer. Read the final decision recorded by the reviewer. The available tools change as the workflow progresses: Investigation: list_incidents , inspect_incident Incident selected: simulate_guardrail_patch Clean replay completed: draft_review_gate Awaiting human decision: the drafting tool is retired, and get_review_status becomes available Decision recorded: the agent can verify the result but cannot create or change it Tools such as approve , reject , activate , and deploy are deliberately never exposed through WebMCP. The human reviewer sees the same synchronized evidence as the agent. They must provide their identity, add a review note, confirm that they examined the evidence, and record their decision using consequence-specific interface controls. The blocked purchase remains unauthorized throughout the process, and the demo never deploys a real external policy. Without WebMCP, an agent would have to scrape a dense incident interface, infer relationships between records, and potentially interact with controls that grant more authority than the task requires. Reviewline replaces that approach with structured capabilities, deterministic evidence IDs, bounded results, explicit labels for untrusted content, a live capability manifest, and an append-only session timeline. How we built it Reviewline is a deterministic, client-only application built with React, TypeScript, and Vite. It uses the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool(...) API and falls back progressively to an in-page Tool Inspector when native WebMCP support is unavailable. The architecture separates: Deterministic domain actions and invariants Shared application state used by both the interface and WebMCP tools Strict runtime input validation Bounded outputs and structured errors Phase-aware tool definitions Lifecycle-safe native tool registration and retirement Every tool handler calls the same validated domain action used by the visible interface. JSON Schema helps the agent understand and invoke tools correctly, but the runtime implementation remains the final authority. The application updates the visible interface before a tool promise resolves. This ensures that the human reviewer and the agent always see the same resulting state. Tool calls, registration changes, results, workflow transitions, and the final human decision are all recorded in the session timeline. The registration layer also handles tool retirement carefully. It stops admitting new calls before retiring a tool generation, allows calls that have already started to finish, and prevents failed or timed-out registration attempts from leaving partially registered tools available. We tested the native browser contract using Chrome 152 rather than relying only on a polyfill. The deployed workflow discovers each dynamic capability manifest, executes the tools available at every phase, records the human decision through the interface, and verifies that forbidden authority tools never appear. The static application is deployed on GitHub Pages. A strict build verifier checks the project subpath, inventories active HTML resources, rejects external or inline executable content, and confirms that real, non-symlinked JavaScript and CSS artifacts exist inside the build directory. Challenges we ran into Defining a real authority boundary The hardest part was not deciding which tools to add. It was proving exactly when a tool should no longer be available. For example, drafting must remain unavailable until a clean replay has been completed. Once the workflow reaches human review, that drafting capability must be retired. Making this boundary explicit—and enforcing it throughout the entire lifecycle—was one of the project’s most important design challenges. Validating the complete state graph Validating only the selected incident or current proposal was not enough. Before retained tools could run safely, we needed to verify canonical IDs, references, actors, timestamps, simulation evidence, audit events, and timeline consistency across the full application state. Handling lifecycle races Native registration and browser testing revealed race conditions that happy-path tests did not catch. These included cancellation, timeouts, retained handles, process cleanup, and stale tool references. We added adversarial tests covering registration retirement, process-spawn failures, first and second termination signals, hanging browser shutdowns, stale tool handles, and fixture cleanup. Proving that the replay was meaningful Blocking the malicious trigger was only half the job. A guardrail that blocks everything would technically stop the incident, but it would not be useful. To avoid that outcome, Reviewline evaluates the triggering case alongside a named benign control. Drafting remains unavailable if the proposed guardrail causes any regression in the benign case. Making the GitHub Pages build portable and trustworthy GitHub Pages serves the application from a project-specific subpath. We needed to verify that every active script and stylesheet used the correct base path and resolved to a real build artifact. The verifier also rejects path traversal, malformed paths, external resources, inline executable content, and symlink escapes. Testing native WebMCP A test double can validate application logic, but it cannot prove that the browser integration behaves correctly. Native testing required us to account for Chrome’s serialized tool arguments and results, dynamic registration timing, cancellation behavior, and synchronization between tool execution and the visible interface. Accomplishments we’re proud of Built a complete WebMCP-native collaboration workflow rather than a generic CRUD-style tool surface Made the principle of least authority visible through a dynamic capability manifest Kept approval, rejection, activation, and deployment entirely outside the agent’s tool surface Added deterministic replay against both a malicious trigger and a named benign control Ensured that agent actions update the same visible state used by the human reviewer Added an append-only session timeline and a human-attributed audit record Preserved a complete human workflow in browsers without native WebMCP support Deployed a public, credential-free demo with no backend or production mutation endpoint Verified the project with: 303 unit, component, and integration tests 33 dedicated lifecycle, workflow, and portable-build tests 13 Playwright end-to-end tests TypeScript type checking and zero-warning linting npm audit with zero vulnerabilities actionlint workflow validation Native
